content: The quality of evidence from systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and non-controlled studies (NCSs) was evaluated separately for high-income countries (HICs) and lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The overall certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) framework, following World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. This process involved evaluating each study outcome for potential risks of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias. For non-randomized studies, the ROBINS-I (Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions) tool was used to inform GRADE ratings, as recommended by recent guidelines. When using ROBINS-I, the initial rating for non-controlled studies was set as high and subsequently downgraded based on specific criteria. For instance, the risk of bias was downgraded once if the response rate was below 80% and twice if it was under 60%. Imprecision was downgraded once for wide confidence intervals or sample sizes below 300 participants and twice for sample sizes below 100. Inconsistency was downgraded once if unexplained heterogeneity between studies was observed, indicated by an I² value greater than 50%. For observational (cross-sectional) studies, the initial rating started as low but could be upgraded if certain factors strengthened the evidence base. These factors included consistency across a large number of studies and participants, the presence of a dose-response relationship, or evidence of an effect despite confounders acting in the opposite direction. For qualitative studies, the GRADE-CERQual (Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research) approach was applied. The GRADE assessments were conducted by one researcher and reviewed by a senior researcher in consultation with the WHO Secretariat and the Guideline Development Group (GDG) methodologist. This methodology was part of the WHO guideline on school health services, specifically detailed in Web Annex D, which focused on systematic reviews of the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive school health services.
